analysis.one_liner: Lets people crushed by medical debt file bankruptcy more easily, keep their homes, and erase medical and student loans.
analysis.headline: The bill has been introduced and sent to two House committees, with one cosponsor; no committee action or vote has been scheduled, and Congress is still in session.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites federal bankruptcy rules for people whose finances were wrecked by medical bills. If a person's unpaid medical costs over three years top roughly 10% of their income (or $10,000, whichever is less), or an illness forced them out of work or into caring for a sick relative, they qualify as a "medically distressed debtor." Those people could skip the income test that usually forces people into Chapter 13 repayment, skip the mandatory credit counseling class, protect up to $250,000 of home value from creditors, wipe out student loans without proving "undue hardship," and keep the bankruptcy off their credit reports entirely. They would have to file a sworn statement of their medical expenses and swear they did not run up bills to game the system [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Households drowning in medical debt — including people who lost jobs or wages because of illness, and people caring for a sick spouse, child, or parent. Roughly 10% of Americans carry medical debt, and people who file bankruptcy because of it would be able to keep their home, erase more debt, and rebuild their finances without a bankruptcy on their credit record for years [S2]. Spouses of qualifying debtors are covered too.

how_it_helps.text: A debtor whose unpaid medical costs over three years exceed the lesser of 10% of adjusted gross income or $10,000 — or who lost wages or a job due to illness, or who had to care for an ill family member — qualifies as a "medically distressed debtor" [S2].
Medically distressed debtors can exempt up to $250,000 in home value (or a burial plot) from creditors, even in states whose own exemption is lower [S2].

They are exempt from the Chapter 7 "means test" — the income screening added in 2005 that pushes many filers into a repayment plan instead of a fresh start — and are exempt from the Chapter 13 rule requiring they commit all disposable income to repay creditors for five years [S2].

They are exempt from the pre-filing credit counseling requirement [S2], and their student loans become dischargeable in bankruptcy without having to prove "undue hardship," the near-impossible standard that currently blocks most student loan discharges [S2].
Their bankruptcy is excluded from consumer credit reports entirely, so it would not appear on the record used by landlords, lenders, and employers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Creditors — hospitals and other health care providers that are owed medical bills, credit card banks, and holders of student loans — would collect less from people who file under these provisions. In practice some of that cost gets spread to other patients and borrowers through pricing and interest rates. Lenders also lose the ability to see a medical bankruptcy on a credit report when deciding whether to extend new credit.

drawbacks.text: Creditors would recover less: medical providers, credit card issuers, and student loan holders would absorb larger losses from qualifying bankruptcy cases [S2].
Keeping a bankruptcy off credit reports entirely removes information lenders use to price risk, which could lead lenders to raise rates for everyone rather than price risk per borrower [S2].
The $250,000 federal homestead exemption applies even where state law is lower, which some states view as overriding their own property rules and could shelter higher-value homes from creditors [S2].

A good-faith objection: easing the means test and credit counseling requirements could allow some households to bypass screening designed to distinguish those who genuinely cannot pay from those who choose not to; the bill relies on a sworn medical-expense statement under penalty of perjury as its main safeguard [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people whose finances were destroyed by an illness — often through no choice of their own — the bill offers a genuine fresh start: keep the house, erase medical and student debt, and avoid a years-long bankruptcy stain on their credit. The costs fall on creditors and are partly passed through to other borrowers and patients, and the bill's safeguards (a sworn attestation) are thinner than the screenings it waives. On balance the benefits go to a defined, vulnerable group rather than broadly, but the terms of the trade-off are real and debatable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary and Financial Services committees on the same day, and neither committee has acted on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen (D-TN) introduced the Medical Bankruptcy Fairness Act of 2026 in the House on July 14, 2026 [S1] [S4].
The bill was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary and, in addition, to the Committee on Financial Services, for consideration of provisions within each committee's jurisdiction [S4].
The bill has one cosponsor, Rep. André Carson (D-IN), who joined as an original sponsor [S3].
No further action — no markup, hearing, floor vote, or Senate companion action — appears in the record as of the latest action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet: the bill is sitting in committee with a two-member Democratic sponsor team and no scheduled action. Hospitals, banks, and student loan holders are currently better off simply because the bill has not moved — none of the new debtor protections are in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; creditors avoid a fight

sides.party_line_note: Only two members are on record so far, both Democrats; no votes have occurred and no opposition has registered, so the partisan shape of the fight is not yet knowable.

industries.note: Medical bills are the debt this bill discharges, so hospitals and provider groups would collect less from patients who file bankruptcy. Their interest in easier collections runs against debtors getting a fresh start.

industries.industry: Consumer debt collectors and credit reporting bureaus
industries.note: The bill excludes medical bankruptcies from consumer reports, cutting off both the reporting bureaus' data streams and collectors' ability to use a bankruptcy record to pursue or price against these debtors.

Medically distressed debtors could discharge student loans without proving undue hardship, a standard that currently blocks nearly all such discharges, so loan holders would face more losses than under current law.
Card debt incurred while paying medical bills would be easier to wipe out, and issuers would lose the credit-report signal, shifting risk across their borrower pools.

analysis.trajectory: This is a late-session bill from a two-member Democratic sponsor team, referred to two committees with no scheduled markup, hearing, or floor action. Bills like this rarely reach the floor in the months left in a Congress unless leadership elevates them; the most likely path is that it sits in committee and expires with the session, though a future Congress could reintroduce it.
